claim: Diurnal oscillation of intracellular redox potential couples metabolism with the circadian clock.
source: Diurnal oscillation of intracellular redox potential is known to couple metabolism with the circadian clock, yet the responsible mechanisms are not well understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge, though the mechanisms are noted as not well understood.

claim: Chemical activation of NRF2 modifies circadian gene expression and rhythmicity.
source: We show here that chemical activation of NRF2 modifies circadian gene expression and rhythmicity, with phenotypes similar to genetic NRF2 activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Nrf2 function in mouse fibroblasts, hepatocytes and liver altered circadian rhythms.
source: Loss of Nrf2 function in mouse fibroblasts, hepatocytes and liver also altered circadian rhythms, suggesting that NRF2 stoichiometry and/or timing of expression are important to timekeeping in some cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: NRF2 stoichiometry and/or timing of expression are important to timekeeping in some cells.
source: Loss of Nrf2 function in mouse fibroblasts, hepatocytes and liver also altered circadian rhythms, suggesting that NRF2 stoichiometry and/or timing of expression are important to timekeeping in some cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding loss of Nrf2 function.

claim: Activation of NRF2 at a circadian time corresponding to the peak generation of endogenous oxidative signals resulted in NRF2-dependent reinforcement of circadian amplitude.
source: Consistent with this concept, activation of NRF2 at a circadian time corresponding to the peak generation of endogenous oxidative signals resulted in NRF2-dependent reinforcement of circadian amplitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Activated NRF2 bound specific enhancer regions of the core clock repressor gene Cry2 in hepatocytes.
source: In hepatocytes, activated NRF2 bound specific enhancer regions of the core clock repressor gene Cry2, increased Cry2 expression and repressed CLOCK/BMAL1-regulated E-box transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 6D.

claim: Activated NRF2 increased Cry2 expression in hepatocytes.
source: In hepatocytes, activated NRF2 bound specific enhancer regions of the core clock repressor gene Cry2, increased Cry2 expression and repressed CLOCK/BMAL1-regulated E-box transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by gene expression data in Figure 6.

claim: Activated NRF2 repressed CLOCK/BMAL1-regulated E-box transcription in hepatocytes.
source: In hepatocytes, activated NRF2 bound specific enhancer regions of the core clock repressor gene Cry2, increased Cry2 expression and repressed CLOCK/BMAL1-regulated E-box transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 6E and 6G.

claim: NRF2 and clock comprise an interlocking loop that integrates cellular redox signals into tissue-specific circadian timekeeping.
source: Together these data indicate that NRF2 and clock comprise an interlocking loop that integrates cellular redox signals into tissue-specific circadian timekeeping.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the abstract, based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Organisms with a circadian period length matched to that of their environment grow faster and have greater reproductive fitness and lifespan than their unsynchronized competitors.
source: Organisms with a circadian period length matched to that of their environment grow faster and have greater reproductive fitness and lifespan than their unsynchronized competitors (Dodd et al., 2005; Woelfle et al., 2004; Ouyang et al., 1998; Beaver et al., 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the anterior hypothalamus are responsible for integrating environmental light-dark input and synchronizing timekeeping in peripheral tissues.
source: The suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) of the anterior hypothalamus represent the top of the hierarchy, responsible for integrating environmental light-dark input and synchronizing timekeeping in peripheral tissues (Liu et al., 2007a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Most tissues possess autonomous cellular oscillators that control rhythmic tissue-specific physiology.
source: Most tissues possess autonomous cellular oscillators that control rhythmic tissue-specific physiology.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: CLOCK/BMAL1 and PER/CRY form a core transcription-translation feedback loop in the circadian clock.
source: At the molecular level, the circadian clock is composed of a core transcription-translation feedback loop, in which transcriptional activators aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator-like (ARNTL/BMAL1) and circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) regulate the transcription of their own repressors, period 1/2/3 (Per1/2/3) and cryptochrome 1/2 (Cry1/2) (Ko and Takahashi, 2006; Reppert and Weaver, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PER and CRY repress their own transcription through the inhibition of the CLOCK/BMAL1 transcriptional complex.
source: PER and CRY repress their own transcription through the inhibition of the CLOCK/BMAL1 transcriptional complex forming the core feedback loop (Zhang and Kay, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RORα/β/γ-dependent transcription of Bmal1 is inhibited by Rev-Erbα/β, forming a stabilizing feedback loop.
source: The fidelity of the core clock loop is stabilized by a second interlocking feedback loop composed of retinoic acid receptor-related orphan receptor (RORα/β/γ)-dependent transcription of Bmal1, a process inhibited by the Bmal1 downstream targets Rev-Erbα/β (Nr1d1/Nr1d2) (Preitner et al., 2002; Sato et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2008; Cho et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The CLOCK/BMAL1-complex regulates the expression of thousands of genes that drive rhythmic changes in tissue-specific physiological and cellular processes.
source: In addition to the regulation of known clock genes, the CLOCK/BMAL1-complex also regulates the expression of thousands of other genes, which drive rhythmic changes in various tissue-specific physiological and cellular processes (Zhang et al., 2014; Perelis et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Many clock controlled output genes encode metabolic enzymes leading to diurnal oscillations in carbohydrate flux.
source: Many clock controlled output genes encode metabolic enzymes leading to diurnal oscillations in carbohydrate flux (Asher and Schibler, 2011; Bass, 2012; Zhang and Kay, 2010; Bass and Takahashi, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Rhythmic carbohydrate catabolism and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in hepatocytes likely contribute to oscillations in reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Rhythmic carbohydrate catabolism and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, particularly in hepatocytes (Jacobi et al., 2015; Peek et al., 2013), likely contribute to oscillations in reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Pekovic-Vaughan et al., 2014; Stangherlin and Reddy, 2013; Milev and Reddy, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature and uses the qualifier 'likely' indicating inference.

claim: Signaling through oxidative intermediates modulates an array of redox sensitive transcription factors and enzymes to regulate gene expression, metabolic flux, and timekeeping.
source: Signaling through oxidative intermediates (Sies, 2014) modulates an array of redox sensitive transcription factors and enzymes to regulate gene expression, metabolic flux, and timekeeping (Pekovic-Vaughan et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Wible and Sutter, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Appropriate timing and magnitude of ROS signaling likely facilitates the temporal segregation and transition between incompatible metabolic processes and increases overall metabolic efficiency.
source: Appropriate timing and magnitude of ROS signaling likely facilitates the temporal segregation and transition between incompatible metabolic processes and increases overall metabolic efficiency (Milev and Reddy, 2015; Jacobi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and uses the qualifier 'likely' indicating inference.

claim: NRF2 is a key transcription factor regulated by oxidative signaling that controls both metabolic and circadian gene expression.
source: A key transcription factor, regulated by oxidative signaling, controlling both metabolic (Mitsuishi et al., 2012) and circadian (Rey et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2014) gene expression is NF-E2 related-factor 2 (NRF2).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The activity of NRF2 is antagonized by the cytoplasmic repressor KEAP1.
source: The activity of NRF2 is antagonized by the cytoplasmic repressor kelch like ECH associated protein 1 (KEAP1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: KEAP1 destabilizes NRF2 by facilitating its ubiquitinylation and eventual proteasomal degradation.
source: KEAP1 destabilizes NRF2 by facilitating its ubiquitinylation and eventual proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activators of NRF2 signaling relieve NRF2 from KEAP1-mediated repression through the oxidation or covalent modification of KEAP1 cysteine residues.
source: Activators of NRF2 signaling relieve NRF2 from KEAP1-mediated repression through the oxidation or covalent modification of KEAP1 cysteine residues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: D3T, CDDO-Im, tBHQ, and H2O2 are well-studied chemical NRF2 activators.
source: Well-studied chemical NRF2 activators include the clinically relevant electrophiles 3H-1,2-dithiole-3-thione (D3T) and 1-[2-cyano-3,12-dioxooleana-1,9 (11)-dien-28-oyl]imidazole (CDDO-Im), and the oxidants tert-butylhydroquinone (tBHQ) (Imhoff and Hansen, 2010) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation for tBHQ and is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Modification of KEAP1 cysteine residues by NRF2 activators results in an increased NRF2 half-life that facilitates nuclear translocation and accumulation.
source: Modification of KEAP1 cysteine residues by these agents results in an increased NRF2 half-life that facilitates nuclear translocation and accumulation (Wible and Sutter, 2017; Suzuki and Yamamoto, 2015; Kwak et al., 2004; Saito et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The expression of Nrf2 is under the transcriptional regulation of the CLOCK/BMAL1-complex.
source: The expression of Nrf2 is under the transcriptional regulation of the CLOCK/BMAL1-complex (Pekovic-Vaughan et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: CLOCK/BMAL1-dependent Nrf2 regulation gives rise to diurnal patterns in NRF2 signaling.
source: CLOCK/BMAL1-dependent Nrf2 regulation gives rise to diurnal patterns in NRF2 signaling, which underlies the rhythmic expression of antioxidant and metabolic enzymes as well as NADPH reducing equivalents and glutathione biosynthesis (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: E-box and D-box-containing clock genes (Nr1d1, Nr1d2, Dbp, Tef, and Per3) were up-regulated in response to D3T in Wt mice.
source: While E-box and D-box-containing clock genes (Nr1d1, Nr1d2, Dbp, Tef, and Per3) were up-regulated in response to D3T in Wt mice, genes that are regulated primarily via RAR-related orphan receptor response elements (ROREs) (Bmal1, Npas2, E4bp4) were down-regulated, consistent with the network features of the molecular clock (Ueda et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2008; Baggs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with cited literature on clock network features.

claim: Genes regulated primarily via ROREs (Bmal1, Npas2, E4bp4) were down-regulated in response to D3T in Wt mice.
source: While E-box and D-box-containing clock genes (Nr1d1, Nr1d2, Dbp, Tef, and Per3) were up-regulated in response to D3T in Wt mice, genes that are regulated primarily via RAR-related orphan receptor response elements (ROREs) (Bmal1, Npas2, E4bp4) were down-regulated, consistent with the network features of the molecular clock (Ueda et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2008; Baggs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with cited literature on clock network features.

claim: The full induction of E-box- and D-box-containing genes (Per3, Nr1d1, Nr1d2, Dbp, and Tef) in response to D3T-treatment required the presence of the KEAP1/NRF2 signaling pathway.
source: The full induction of E-box- and D-box-containing genes (Per3, Nr1d1, Nr1d2, Dbp, and Tef) in response to D3T-treatment required the presence of the KEAP1/NRF2 signaling pathway, as their induction was significantly compromised in Nrf2-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A comparing Wt and Nrf2-/- mice.

claim: Nrf2 deficiency did not alter the down-regulation of Bmal1, Cry1, or E4bp4 in response to D3T.
source: Nrf2 deficiency did not alter the down-regulation of Bmal1, Cry1, or E4bp4, suggesting their independence of NRF2 and that the circadian network effect did not transmit to RORE-mediated transcription.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and the authors' interpretation.

claim: Treatment with 100 μM D3T resulted in significantly reduced rhythm amplitude in Wt MEFs, an effect that was not observed in Nrf2-/- cells.
source: Both treatments resulted in significantly reduced rhythm amplitude, an effect that was not observed in the Nrf2-/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Treatment with 50 μM tBHQ resulted in significantly reduced rhythm amplitude in Wt MEFs, an effect that was not observed in Nrf2-/- cells.
source: Both treatments resulted in significantly reduced rhythm amplitude, an effect that was not observed in the Nrf2-/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with 100 μM H2O2 resulted in significant NRF2-dependent reductions in rhythm amplitude in MEFs.
source: Similar to both D3T and tBHQ treatment, we observed significant NRF2-dependent reductions in rhythm amplitude in the presence of H2O2.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Treatment with CDDO-Im caused significant reductions in both amplitude and period length in Wt MEFs that were absent in Nrf2-/- MEFs.
source: Treatment with CDDO-Im caused significant reductions in both amplitude and period length (Treatment), that were noticeably absent in Nrf2-/- MEFs.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The restoration of normal circadian rhythmicity in CDDO-Im treated Wt cells after removal of treatment confirmed good cell health and dependency on CDDO-Im for the observed alterations.
source: The restoration of normal circadian rhythmicity in the treated Wt cells served as a confirmation of good cell health and a dependency on CDDO-Im for the alterations in the circadian parameters observed.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 (Recovery phase).

claim: Nrf2-/- MEFs display inherently low bioluminescence rhythm amplitudes.
source: In our earlier experiments, we observed inherently low bioluminescence rhythm amplitudes (Figure 1B–D) in Nrf2-/- MEFs, indicating that NRF2 may be a required component of the circadian clockwork.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: The loss of Nrf2 resulted in a significant decrease in period length in MEFs.
source: In addition to the previously observed reduction in rhythm amplitude, the loss of Nrf2 also resulted in a significant decrease in period length (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The restoration of Nrf2 expression rescued both circadian amplitude and period length relative to the parental Nrf2-/- cell line.
source: The restoration of Nrf2 expression rescued both circadian amplitude and period length relative to the parental Nrf2-/- cell line, but fell short of achieving Wt rhythmicity.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Exogenous Nrf2 expression yields functional NRF2 protein as confirmed by increased Nqo1 expression.
source: As a marker of NRF2 activity, we measured increased Nqo1 expression, confirming that exogenous Nrf2 expression yields functional NRF2 protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NRF2 protein expression in the rescued cell line was constitutively elevated at 24 hr and 36 hr post-synchronization.
source: Consistent with Nrf2 expression being driven by a constitutive CMV promoter, NRF2 protein expression in the rescued cell line was constitutively elevated at 24 hr and 36 hr post-synchronization.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Wt MEFs show circadian NRF2 expression.
source: This contrasted with circadian NRF2 expression observed in Wt MEFs (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: shRNA-mediated Nrf2 knockdown in MEFs led to significant reductions in both rhythm amplitude and period length.
source: Nrf2 knockdown led to significant reductions in both rhythm amplitude and period length (Figure 2E), albeit to a lesser extent than what was observed in Nrf2-/- MEFs.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nr1d1 expression was decreased in response to shNrf2.
source: Interestingly, Nr1d1 expression was also decreased in response to shNrf2, consistent with previous reports (Rey et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2014) and our results from mouse liver (Figure 1A), suggesting that Nr1d1 may be transcriptionally regulated by NRF2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2G and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The peak of NR1D1 protein accumulation was delayed by 4 hr in Nrf2-/- MEFs relative to Wt.
source: In Nrf2-/- MEFs, the peak of NR1D1 protein accumulation was delayed by 4 hr relative to the Wt (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Delayed NR1D1 expression in Nrf2-/- cells suggests that Nr1d1 is likely regulated by additional transcription factors beyond NRF2.
source: Delayed NR1D1 expression, as opposed to the complete loss, in Nrf2-/- cells suggests that Nr1d1 is likely regulated by additional transcription factors beyond NRF2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The improper temporal regulation of NR1D1 in the absence of Nrf2 may contribute to the perturbed circadian rhythmicity observed in MEFs lacking Nrf2.
source: The improper temporal regulation of NR1D1 in the absence of Nrf2, however, may contribute to the perturbed circadian rhythmicity observed in MEFs lacking Nrf2.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Genetic or chemical inhibition of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) altered circadian period length in a NRF2-dependent manner.
source: A recent report demonstrated that that genetic or chemical inhibition of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) altered circadian period length in a NRF2-dependent manner (Rey et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Constitutive NRF2 activation in the Keap1-/- background resulted in significant reductions in both amplitude and period length.
source: Constitutive NRF2 activation in the Keap1-/- background resulted in significant reductions in both amplitude and period length (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Overexpression of NRF2 in a Wt background resulted in reduced circadian amplitude and period length in manner similar to the Keap1-/- cell line.
source: Overexpression of NRF2 in a Wt background resulted in reduced circadian amplitude and period length in manner similar to the Keap1-/- cell line (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Elevated levels of NR1D1 protein and RNA were observed in response to Nrf2 overexpression.
source: Moreover, we observed elevated levels of NR1D1 protein (Figure 3C) and RNA (Figure 3D) in response to Nrf2 overexpression, consistent with NRF2 contributing to Nr1d1 gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The circadian phenotypes resulting from the overexpression of NRF2 recapitulated the phenotype of genetically rescued Nrf2-/- MEFs.
source: Interestingly, the circadian phenotypes resulting from the overexpression of NRF2 recapitulated the phenotype of genetically rescued Nrf2-/- MEFs, suggesting that the timing or absolute stoichiometry of NRF2 protein abundance are likely to be important for proper circadian function.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing data from Figures 2B and 3B.

claim: The timing or absolute stoichiometry of NRF2 protein abundance are likely to be important for proper circadian function.
source: Interestingly, the circadian phenotypes resulting from the overexpression of NRF2 recapitulated the phenotype of genetically rescued Nrf2-/- MEFs, suggesting that the timing or absolute stoichiometry of NRF2 protein abundance are likely to be important for proper circadian function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: In response to 100 μM D3T, the expression of both Nqo1 and Nr1d1 were significantly induced in Wt MEFs.
source: In response to 100 μM D3T, the expression of both Nqo1 and Nr1d1 were significantly induced (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The induction of Nqo1 and Nr1d1 by D3T was absent in D3T-treated Nrf2-/- MEFs.
source: These effects were noticeably absent in D3T-treated Nrf2-/- MEFs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A slight but significant induction of Nr1d1 expression was observed in Nrf2-/- MEFs in the absence of D3T-treatment.
source: We did observe a slight, but significant, induction of Nr1d1 expression in Nrf2-/- MEFs in the absence of D3T-treatment, consistent with the previously reported induction of Nr1d1 under oxidative intracellular conditions (Yang et al., 2014), a condition likely to be present in Nrf2-/- MEFs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation of NRF2 in D3T-treated MEFs demonstrated direct binding of NRF2 to two of the three ARE elements identified in the Nr1d1 promoter (Nr1d1-2 and Nr1d1-3).
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation of NRF2 in MEFs treated with 100 μM D3T for 24 hr demonstrated direct binding of NRF2 to two of the three ARE elements identified in the Nr1d1 promoter, namely Nr1d1-2 and Nr1d1-3, and two ARE elements in Nqo1, namely Nqo1-1 and Nqo1-2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation of NRF2 in D3T-treated MEFs demonstrated direct binding of NRF2 to two ARE elements in Nqo1 (Nqo1-1 and Nqo1-2).
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation of NRF2 in MEFs treated with 100 μM D3T for 24 hr demonstrated direct binding of NRF2 to two of the three ARE elements identified in the Nr1d1 promoter, namely Nr1d1-2 and Nr1d1-3, and two ARE elements in Nqo1, namely Nqo1-1 and Nqo1-2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The binding of NRF2 to the element Nr1d1-3 is a novel finding.
source: The binding of NRF2 to the elements Nr1d1-3 and Nqo1-1 are novel findings, while the binding of NRF2 to the element in Nr1d1-2 (Yang et al., 2014) and Nqo1-1 (Nioi et al., 2003) confirm previous reports.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the ChIP-PCR data.

claim: The binding of NRF2 to the element Nqo1-1 is a novel finding.
source: The binding of NRF2 to the elements Nr1d1-3 and Nqo1-1 are novel findings, while the binding of NRF2 to the element in Nr1d1-2 (Yang et al., 2014) and Nqo1-1 (Nioi et al., 2003) confirm previous reports.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the ChIP-PCR data.

claim: The binding of NRF2 to the element Nr1d1-2 confirms previous reports.
source: The binding of NRF2 to the elements Nr1d1-3 and Nqo1-1 are novel findings, while the binding of NRF2 to the element in Nr1d1-2 (Yang et al., 2014) and Nqo1-1 (Nioi et al., 2003) confirm previous reports.
evidence: This is stated as confirming previous reports cited in the text.

claim: Levels of hyperoxidized PRDX were maximal 28 hr post-synchronization in MMH-D3 hepatocytes.
source: Levels of hyperoxidized PRDX were maximal 28 hr post-synchronization (red arrow), which preceded peak NRF2 protein accumulation (black arrow) by 12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Peak NRF2 protein accumulation occurred 40 hr post-synchronization in MMH-D3 hepatocytes, 12 hr after peak PRDX hyperoxidation.
source: Levels of hyperoxidized PRDX were maximal 28 hr post-synchronization (red arrow), which preceded peak NRF2 protein accumulation (black arrow) by 12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 12 hr lag phase between oxidative signaling and NRF2 accumulation is likely a product of the kinetics of NRF2 activation.
source: This 12 hr lag phase is likely a product of the kinetics of NRF2 activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal data.

claim: The timing of oxidative signaling in MMH-D3 hepatocytes is consistent with what has been previously observed in mouse liver.
source: The timing of oxidative signaling (Figure 4A), however, is consistent with what has been previously observed in mouse liver (Xu et al., 2012; Edgar et al., 2012), indicating that the generation of endogenous oxidative signals occurs at a similar time in vitro relative to Nrf2 expression as it does in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the data in Figure 4A with cited literature.

claim: Activation of NRF2 by 100 μM H2O2 at a circadian time corresponding to endogenous peak oxidative signaling resulted in significantly increased amplitude without affecting period length in Wt MEFs.
source: Activation of NRF2 in response to an oxidative signal at this time resulted in significantly increased amplitude, without affecting period length.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A similar amplitude reinforcement effect was observed with D3T treatment.
source: A similar effect was also observed in the presence of another NRF2-activating compound D3T (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that amplitude reinforcement is a function of NRF2 activity and not a side-effect of any one particular chemical.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Amplitude reinforcement is a function of NRF2 activity and not a side-effect of any one particular chemical.
source: A similar effect was also observed in the presence of another NRF2-activating compound D3T (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that amplitude reinforcement is a function of NRF2 activity and not a side-effect of any one particular chemical.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on observing similar effects with different NRF2 activators.

claim: Activation of NRF2 by H2O2 resulted in a subtle advance of the circadian phase.
source: In addition to reinforcing circadian amplitude, activation of NRF2 by H2O2 at this time also resulted in a subtle advance of the circadian phase, which became more prominent at higher concentrations of H2O2 (500 μM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Treatment with 100 μM H2O2 resulted in circadian amplitude reinforcement in Wt MEFs, which was absent in H2O2-treated Nrf2-/- MEFs.
source: Treatment with H2O2, again, resulted in circadian amplitude reinforcement, which was absent in H2O2-treated Nrf2-/- MEFs (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Reinforcement of circadian amplitude following the addition of H2O2 could be blocked in the presence of N-acetylcysteine (NAC).
source: Reinforcement of circadian amplitude, following the addition of H2O2, could be blocked in the presence of an antioxidant (N-acetylcysteine; NAC) (Figure 4D), suggesting that oxidation was indeed the relevant signal responsible for the reinforcement of circadian amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Treatment with NAC alone resulted in significantly decreased rhythm amplitude and period length.
source: Interestingly, treatment with NAC alone resulted in significantly decreased rhythm amplitude and period length, suggesting that endogenous oxidative signals (Sies, 2017) may play a role in the maintenance of circadian timekeeping.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Endogenous oxidative signals may play a role in the maintenance of circadian timekeeping.
source: Interestingly, treatment with NAC alone resulted in significantly decreased rhythm amplitude and period length, suggesting that endogenous oxidative signals (Sies, 2017) may play a role in the maintenance of circadian timekeeping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NAC treatment data with support from cited literature.

claim: Addition of H2O2 prior to the trough of PER2 expression resulted in a subtle delay of the circadian phase.
source: In contrast to what we observed when applying H2O2 prior to the peak of PER2 expression, addition of H2O2 prior to the trough resulted in a subtle delay of the circadian phase.
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When H2O2 was added at the nadir of PER2 expression, the circadian phase appeared to be delayed or possibly reset.
source: Interestingly, when H2O2 was added to the cultures at the nadir of PER2 expression, the circadian phase appeared to be delayed or possibly reset (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: H2O2-induced phase-dependent shifts in circadian phase may occur through an NRF2-dependent mechanism.
source: This effect was not observed in Nrf2-/- MEFs, indicating that H2O2-induced phase-dependent shifts in circadian phase may occur through an NRF2-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 4F comparing Wt and Nrf2-/- MEFs.

claim: Shifts in circadian phase in response to oxidative signals have been observed previously across multiple cell lines.
source: While shifts in circadian phase in response to oxidative signals have been observed previously across multiple cell lines (Tahara et al., 2016; Putker et al., 2018), our data implicates the activation of NRF2 as the likely mechanism through which oxidants signal into the clockwork.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The activation of NRF2 is the likely mechanism through which oxidants signal into the clockwork.
source: While shifts in circadian phase in response to oxidative signals have been observed previously across multiple cell lines (Tahara et al., 2016; Putker et al., 2018), our data implicates the activation of NRF2 as the likely mechanism through which oxidants signal into the clockwork.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: shRNA-mediated Nrf2 knockdown in hepatocytes caused significant amplitude and period length reductions.
source: Similar to our observations in MEFs, shRNA-mediated Nrf2 knockdown in hepatocytes caused significant amplitude and period length reductions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hepatocytes harboring shNrf2 showed a 50% reduction in total NRF2 protein expression and a greater than 90% reduction in NQO1.
source: Hepatocytes harboring shNrf2 showed a 50% reduction in total NRF2 protein expression and a greater than 90% reduction in NQO1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Loss of Nrf2 in the liver of mice from both MYM and YWK strains resulted in a significant alteration in circadian period length.
source: Loss of Nrf2 in the liver of mice from both strains resulted in a significant alteration in circadian period length (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data from liver organotypic slices shown in Figures 5C and 5E.

claim: No deleterious effects of Nrf2 loss on circadian rhythmicity were observed in the lung tissue of either MYM or YWK strain.
source: Surprisingly, we observed no deleterious effects of Nrf2 loss on circadian rhythmicity in the lung tissue of either strain (Figure 5D and F), despite earlier literature indicating that NRF2 is a circadian output in the lung (Pekovic-Vaughan et al., 2014) and can be integrated into clock function in that tissue type in response to stress (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data from lung organotypic slices shown in Figures 5D and 5F.

claim: The loss of Nrf2 had no effect on the locomotor behavioral activity in mice.
source: Previous reports have indicated that the loss of Nrf2 had no effect on the locomotor behavioral activity in mice (Pekovic-Vaughan et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: No significant alteration in circadian rhythmicity was observed in SCN organotypic slices from the YWK strain of Nrf2-null mice.
source: In agreement with this observation, we observed no significant alteration in circadian rhythmicity in SCN organotypic slices from the YWK strain of Nrf2-null mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data from SCN organotypic slices shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nrf2 overexpression in MMH-D3 hepatocytes resulted in decreased rhythm amplitude and period length.
source: Similar to our observations in MEFs, Nrf2 overexpression resulted in decreased rhythm amplitude and period length (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Nrf2 overexpression led to significantly elevated Nqo1, Cry2, and Nr1d1 expression in MMH-D3 hepatocytes.
source: Nrf2 overexpression also led to significantly elevated Nqo1, Cry2, and Nr1d1 expression (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: D3T-induced activation of NRF2 in hepatocytes caused significant increases in Cry2, Nr1d1, and Nqo1 RNA expression.
source: Consistent with the effect of genetic gain-of-function, D3T-induced activation of NRF2 in hepatocytes caused significant increases in Cry2, Nr1d1, and Nqo1 RNA expression (Figure 6C), suggesting these genes may be under NRF2 regulation.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation of NRF2 in D3T-treated hepatocytes demonstrated significantly elevated binding of NRF2 to novel enhancer elements in the promoters of Cry2, Nr1d1, and Nqo1.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation of NRF2 in D3T-treated hepatocytes demonstrated significantly elevated binding of NRF2 to novel enhancer elements in the promoters of Cry2, Nr1d1, and Nqo1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: D3T-induced enhanced binding of NRF2 to ARE elements previously characterized in Nr1d1 and Nqo1 was observed.
source: In addition to these novel elements, we also observed D3T-induced enhanced binding of NRF2 to ARE elements previously characterized in Nr1d1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Yang et al., 2014) and Nqo1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Nioi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Transfection of pLV7-Nrf2 into HEK293T cells was able to repress CLOCK/BMAL1-mediated transcription of Per1:Luc and synthetic E-box:Luc reporter constructs.
source: Along with these effects on circadian gene expression, transfection of pLV7-Nrf2 into HEK293T cells was able to repress CLOCK/BMAL1-mediated transcription of Per1:Luc and synthetic E-box:Luc reporter constructs in a manner similar to what was observed in response to the transfection of Cry1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Significant increases in both Cry2 and Nqo1 expression were measured in HEK293T cells transfected with pLenti-Nrf2.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we measured significant increases in both Cry2 and Nqo1 expression in HEK293T cells transfected with pLenti-Nrf2 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Expression of either Cry1/2 or Nrf2 resulted in significant repression of CLOCK/BMAL1 transcriptional activity in HEK293T cells.
source: Expression of either Cry1/2 or Nrf2 resulted in significant repression of CLOCK/BMAL1 transcriptional activity (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Both circadian parameters of rhythm amplitude and period length decreased as a function of D3T dose escalation in MMH-D3 hepatocytes.
source: Both circadian parameters of rhythm amplitude and period length decreased as a function of D3T dose escalation (Figure 6H), while having no measurable negative effect on cell health (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bioluminescence data shown in Figure 6H and cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: D3T dose escalation led to the dose-dependent induction of Nqo1 and Cry2 expression in MMH-D3 hepatocytes.
source: Interestingly, the same D3T dose escalation that produced reductions in rhythm amplitude and period length also led to the dose-dependent induction of Nqo1 and Cry2 expression (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: NRF2 likely represses CLOCK/BMAL1-mediated transcription indirectly through the regulation of Cry2 and Nr1d1 expression.
source: Together, these data support the concept that NRF2 likely represses CLOCK/BMAL1-mediated transcription indirectly through the regulation of Cry2 and Nr1d1 expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the collective experimental findings.

claim: NRF2 and clock comprise an interlocking loop that integrates cellular redox signals into circadian timekeeping.
source: Given the reported E-Box-mediated circadian regulation of Nrf2 (Pekovic-Vaughan et al., 2014), these results indicate that NRF2 and clock comprise an interlocking loop (Figure 6J) that integrates cellular redox signals into circadian timekeeping.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on the collective experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Redox rhythms, including oscillations in H2O2 and hyperoxidized peroxiredoxin, exist across all domains of life.
source: Redox rhythms, including oscillations in H2O2 and hyperoxidized peroxiredoxin (Edgar et al., 2012), exist across all domains of life and are believed to cross-talk with the molecular clock.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Changes in the intracellular redox potential may be the link coupling metabolism to the clock.
source: Parallels between these redox oscillations, metabolic cycles, and circadian gene expression led to the idea that changes in the intracellular redox potential may be the link coupling metabolism to the clock (Putker and O'Neill, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Increases in the NAD+/NADH ratio resulted in reduced CLOCK/BMAL1 DNA-binding affinity in biochemical assays.
source: In biochemical assays, increases in the NAD+/NADH ratio, to mimic an oxidized intracellular environment, resulted in reduced CLOCK/BMAL1 DNA-binding affinity (Rutter et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The levels of zCry1 and zPer2 were elevated in zebrafish Z3 cells in response to light-induced H2O2 production.
source: Additionally, the levels of zCry1 and zPer2 were elevated in zebrafish Z3 cells in response to light-induced H2O2 production (Hirayama et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A single H2O2 bolus recapitulated the elevation of zCry1 and zPer2 levels in zebrafish Z3 cells, confirming that H2O2 was a circadian input signal.
source: A single H2O2 bolus recapitulated these effects, confirming that H2O2 was indeed a circadian input signal.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature (Hirayama et al., 2007).

claim: A previous study reported a NRF2-binding site in the promoter of the clock gene Nr1d1 and its subsequent regulation in response to H2O2 and sulforaphane.
source: A previous study reported a NRF2-binding site in the promoter of the clock gene Nr1d1 and its subsequent regulation in response to H2O2 and sulforaphane (Yang et al., 2014), a well-characterized NRF2 activator (Kensler et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genetic gain-of-function and chemical activation have been shown to lead to distinct NRF2-dependent gene responses.
source: Because genetic gain-of-function and chemical activation have been shown to lead to distinct NRF2-dependent gene responses (Yates et al., 2009), we explored the effects of genetic NRF2 activation on circadian rhythmicity and gene expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NRF2 is emerging as a key regulator of metabolism through the regulation of the PPP and by directing glutamine breakdown into glutathione biosynthetic pathways.
source: Activation of NRF2 is emerging as a key regulator of metabolism through the regulation of the PPP and by directing glutamine breakdown into glutathione biosynthetic pathways (Mitsuishi et al., 2012; Hayes and Dinkova-Kostova, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NRF2-dependent regulation of the PPP suggests that NRF2 may be a contributor in the daily transition between catabolic and anabolic metabolism.
source: NRF2-dependent regulation of the PPP suggests that NRF2 may be a contributor in the daily transition between catabolic and anabolic metabolism.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the known role of NRF2 in PPP regulation.

claim: The coordinated integration of metabolism, redox homeostasis, and the circadian clock in mammals through NRF2 is a mechanism to align energy production and utilization to the environmental light-dark cycle.
source: We propose that the coordinated integration of metabolism, redox homeostasis, and the circadian clock in mammals through NRF2 is a mechanism to align energy production and utilization to the environmental light-dark cycle, as has been observed in plants (Dodd et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and comparison to plants, supported by a citation.

claim: Circadian amplitude and period length are largely dependent on CRY repression of CLOCK/BMAL1-mediated E-box gene transcription.
source: Circadian amplitude and period length are largely dependent on CRY repression of CLOCK/BMAL1-mediated E-box gene transcription, placing the regulation of Cry at the heart of the clock mechanism (Sato et al., 2006; Kume et al., 1999; Reppert and Weaver, 2002; Griffin et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Little is known about the transcriptional regulation of Cry2.
source: Despite its role in the clockwork, little is known about the transcriptional regulation of Cry2.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: NRF2-dependent regulation of Cry2 is a mechanism to relay timing information from the redox oscillator into the molecular clock.
source: Our characterization of a NRF2-binding site in the Cry2 promoter, in addition to its induction, supports the idea that NRF2-dependent regulation of Cry2 is a mechanism to relay timing information from the redox oscillator into the molecular clock.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Both CRY2 and NR1D1 are important regulators of nuclear hormone receptors, governing lipid, glucose, and xenobiotic metabolism.
source: Beyond being NRF2-dependent E-box repressors, both CRY2 and NR1D1 are also important regulators of nuclear hormone receptors, governing lipid, glucose, and xenobiotic metabolism (Zhang et al., 2015; Kriebs et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NRF2-dependent regulation of the production of reducing equivalents through the PPP and heme levels through heme oxygenase one expression further integrate metabolism and the clock mechanism.
source: Additional NRF2-dependent regulation of the production of reducing equivalents through the PPP (Mitsuishi et al., 2012) and heme levels through heme oxygenase one expression (Ishii et al., 2000), which serve as cofactors for CRY2 and NR1D1, respectively, further integrate metabolism and the clock mechanism and highlight the interconnectedness of these oscillators.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: As an E-box-regulated circadian output, NRF2 likely represses its own transcription through the regulation of Cry2 and subsequent CRY2-mediated repression of CLOCK/BMAL1.
source: As an E-box-regulated circadian output (Pekovic-Vaughan et al., 2014), the data presented here suggest that NRF2 likely represses its own transcription through the regulation of Cry2 and subsequent CRY2-mediated repression of CLOCK/BMAL1, thus forming a redox-responsive transcription-translation feedback loop interlocked with the core molecular circadian mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of cited literature.

claim: NRF2 appears to be a key mechanistic link between circadian oscillations in redox balance and clock gene expression rhythms.
source: From these observations, NRF2 appears to be a key mechanistic link between circadian oscillations in redox balance and clock gene expression rhythmns.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Reciprocal integration of redox potential and the clock through NRF2-dependent regulation reinforces the efficiency of both the circadian and metabolic oscillators, contributing to enhanced organismal fitness.
source: Reciprocal integration of redox potential and the clock through NRF2-dependent regulation reinforces the efficiency of both the circadian and metabolic oscillators, contributing to enhanced organismal fitness.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.
